newsitem.title: USA: Environmental battle for lead still not over.
newsitem.headline: Environmental battle for lead still not over.

text.p: The lead industry has notched up key successes in its battle against environmental regulations, but the fight is not over as a government safety agency may step up scrutiny and politicians reach out for the green vote, members of the U.S. Lead Industries Association were told.
"This has been an on-going battle over the years to meet compliance and meet new standards," Gregory Stevens, vice chairman of the LIA to the association's annual meeting.
"These times have been relatively mild in terms of environmental standpoint compared with the past, but we must not be complacent," Stevens said.
President Clinton and Vice President Al Gore, now back for a second term, will push hard on environmental issues.

Gore, a longstanding champion of environmental issues, would also be a presidential candidate in the next election for the White House and will need to recognise the efforts of his support groups, Stevens said.

The LIA helped to cut blood lead levels in children and in the workforce, Stevens said, but the industry still needed to get its message across that there were economic benefits from the lead industry.

In a separate address, Richard Fairfax, deputy director of compliance at the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, OSHA, said the agency is considering a new program to tackle lead exposure in general industry.
At present OSHA has one lead program, exposure of workers to the poisonous metal in the construction industry where there were still problems of fairly high blood lead levels, Fairfax said.
Blood lead levels in the general population were now less of a concern. "The Center for Disease Control data looks good and we are happy with that," Fairfax told Reuters.

Fairfax said that this week's confirmation of Alexis Herman as Labor Secretary, the government department which oversees OSHA, will result in a selection of a new head for the safety agency and, within 5 to 6 months, finalizing new programs.

Fairfax said looking at lead in general industry was among a bunch of issues considered as possible new programs, and it was important that the LIA and lead companies provided input to help OSHA decide whether to include lead in new programs.
OSHA asked for but did not get any comments from the LIA when it drew up the existing lead in construction industry program, Fairfax said.

OSHA has also been asked by Clinton to "save the big stick" approach of heavily fining companies that violate safety regulations, and to seek a more cooperative, voluntary way for companies to comply, Fairfax said.
Fairfax comended the LIA for helping to reduce blood lead levels more rapidly than if OSHA had had to resort to a plethora of new rules and regulations.
